entries.narration: Let's start with the application we will follow through the whole course: a small online shop. A shopper opens the page for product p one thousand and one. The browser asks Route fifty three, the D N S service, for the shop's address, then sends an H T T P S request to a load balancer. The load balancer passes it to one of our app servers, which reads the product from the orders database and links to its image in object storage. Three ideas sit inside that picture. First, every one of those resources is on demand. We create it with an A P I call, and we pay while it exists, not for a machine we bought. Second, some of them are managed services. We never patch the load balancer, and A W S runs the database engine; we only configure them. Third, elasticity. Look at the chart. One app server handles a hundred and fifty requests a second. Overnight, demand is sixty. During the day it is two hundred and forty, and on a sale evening it reaches five hundred and sixty. If we size for the peak, we run four servers all day, which is ninety six server hours. If capacity follows demand, we run one server for eight hours, two for ten, and four for six, which is fifty two server hours, about forty six percent fewer. Now the misconception. The cloud does not scale by itself. You write the scaling rules, a new server takes minutes to be ready, so the evening rise must be anticipated, and account quotas put a ceiling on how many you can start. So the operating model changes who buys hardware, but you still own the design, the configuration, and the bill.

Every A W S service splits the work between two owners, and the split is worth knowing before anything goes wrong. A W S is responsible for security of the cloud: the buildings, the hardware, the host operating systems, and the virtualisation layer that runs your instances. You are responsible for security in the cloud: how you configure things, the code you deploy, who you let in, and your data. The important part is that the line moves with the service. Read the matrix for our ordering app. Our app servers run on E C two, which is infrastructure as a service, so we patch the guest operating system, we install the software, and we set the network rules around each instance. The database runs on R D S. There, A W S patches the operating system and the database engine, but it does so in a maintenance window we choose, and the tables and S Q L are still ours. A Lambda function goes further: A W S runs the runtime, and we own the code and its permissions. S three has no servers for us at all. Yet look at the bottom two rows. Who may access the data, and how it is backed up, are ours for every service on the board. The list on the right turns this into incidents. An unpatched operating system on an app server is our problem. A bucket policy that allows public reads is our problem. A failed disk under the database host is A W S's problem. The misconception to avoid is that managed means secure. A managed service runs correctly, but it does exactly what you configured it to do. So the summary is simple: access and data are always yours, and everything else depends on the service you chose.

Every resource you create lives somewhere, and where it lives decides what can take it down. A Region is a geographic area with its own copy of the services and its own endpoints. Our shop runs in E U west two, which is London. Inside a Region are Availability Zones, groups of data centres with separate power, cooling and networking, close enough for fast links but far enough apart that one local failure should not reach the others. E U west two has three. One small trap: the names A, B and C can point at different physical zones in different accounts in some Regions, so when accounts must agree, they compare zone I Ds instead. Now place the parts of our app. An app server is zonal; it lives in exactly one zone. An S three bucket is Regional; A W S spreads it across zones for us. Our single orders database is placed in one zone, which matters later. And some services are global, outside any one Region: I A M, Route fifty three, and CloudFront. Now the arithmetic. At the evening peak we need four app servers. If we run one per zone, that is three, which is already short, and if a zone fails only two remain. If we run two per zone, that is six. Lose a zone and four remain, which carries the peak. Those two extra servers are the price of surviving a zone failure, and you pay it every hour. The misconception is that multi A Z makes you unstoppable. A Region-wide problem, a bad deployment, or deleted data reaches every zone at once. So decide which boundary you must survive, and pay for exactly the spare capacity that survival needs.

Before we create anything, we need a safe way in. An A W S account is a container: it holds resources, it receives one bill, and it draws a boundary around permissions. Every account has a root user, the email address that created it, and the root user can do everything, including closing the account. So we protect it with multi factor authentication, which A W S now enforces for root users, and we use it only for the handful of tasks that truly need it. Organizations can go further and remove root credentials from member accounts entirely. Daily work happens through I A M Identity Center instead. Follow alex, a developer joining the shop's development account. On the left is alex's configuration. It names the sign-in portal, the account, four four four four, five five five five, six six six six, and the role called ShopDeveloper. Running a w s s s o login opens a browser, where alex enters a password and an M F A code. Then a w s s t s get caller identity asks the Security Token Service a simple question: who am I? Look at the answer. The A R N says assumed role. Alex is not a user with a stored key; alex is holding temporary credentials for a role, and by default that role session lasts one hour, configurable up to twelve, before it must be renewed. The misconception is that an access key in a file is simpler. It is simpler, until it leaks. A long-term key never expires, and it works for whoever finds it. Temporary credentials expire on their own. So the pattern is: root locked away, and people working through one sign-in that hands out short sessions.

Whether you click in the console, type in the C L I, or call an S D K from code, the same thing happens underneath: a signed H T T P S request to an A W S service A P I. Learn to read one, and you can read them all. Take this command. It asks S three, using head object, whether the product file for p one thousand and one exists, and for its metadata, without downloading the body. Read it in three parts. Who: the shop dev profile, which supplies the temporary credentials from our last section. Where: the Region, E U west two, which selects the London endpoint. What: one key in one bucket. Now follow the list. The C L I finds the credentials for the profile. It signs the request with Signature Version four, which binds the signature to the key, the Region and the service. The request travels over H T T P S to the Regional S three endpoint. There, I A M checks whether this identity is allowed the action s three get object on that object's A R N. Head object needs the same permission as reading the object. If it is allowed, we get two hundred O K with headers only: one thousand eight hundred and thirty four bytes, J S O N, and encrypted at rest, which S three does by default for new objects. Notice the A R N shapes on the right. An A R N names a resource exactly, but not every A R N carries every field. S three bucket names are global, so their A R Ns have no Region and no account. I A M is global, so its A R Ns have no Region. A DynamoDB table carries both. The misconception is that the console is a separate system. It calls the same A P Is, under the same permission checks. So every call reduces to identity, Region, resource and action, and the answer is a response or an error that tells you which of the four went wrong.

The last foundation is money, because in the cloud every resource you create is a charge until you delete it. The core rule is that charges follow what exists, not only what is running. Look at the ledger for the shop's development environment. The rates here are hypothetical, chosen to make the arithmetic clear, so check the current pricing pages before you rely on any number. With seven hundred and thirty hours in a month, the running environment costs thirty six dollars and twenty one cents. Now stop the app instance. The compute charge, twenty nine dollars twenty, disappears. But seven dollars and one cent remains, because the thirty gigabyte volume still exists, the Elastic I P is still reserved, the snapshot is still stored, and the product images are still in S three. Stopping is not deleting. To see costs by purpose, we tag resources: project equals shop, environment equals dev, owner equals alex. A tag only appears in cost reports once it is activated as a cost allocation tag, so do that early. Then a budget. Set one for the account, with an alert when actual spending passes eighty percent, and another when the forecast passes one hundred. Here is the misconception. A budget is not a spending cap. Budget data is updated up to three times a day, so an alert can arrive after the money is spent. Budget actions can apply a restrictive policy or stop specific E C two or R D S instances, but they only touch what you configured, and charges like storage keep accruing. So: tag on creation, alert early, and delete what you no longer need. With safe access, a request path, and a ledger, we are ready to make identities and permissions explicit, which is the next chapter.

Every request to A W S is made by a principal, and the first question is always who that principal is. A principal can be the root user, an I A M user with long-term credentials, a session of an I A M role holding temporary credentials, or an A W S service acting for you, such as E C two. Two words get confused here. Authentication proves who you are: a password and an M F A code. Authorisation decides what that proven identity may do, and the rest of this chapter is about authorisation. For people, the modern pattern is federation. A W S does not keep its own password for alex; it trusts the sign-in of the shop's workforce identity provider, through I A M Identity Center. Look at the board. Alex and sam live in the identity source, in groups. Identity Center holds assignments, and an assignment is three things: a group, an account, and a permission set, which is a template of policies. Developers get ShopDeveloper in the dev account, but only ShopReadOnly in production. Operators get ShopOperator in production. When you make an assignment, Identity Center creates a real I A M role in that account, named A W S Reserved S S O followed by the permission set's name and a suffix, and attaches the set's policies. So when alex signs in, alex is not an I A M user anywhere; alex becomes a session of one of those roles. The misconception is that every person needs an I A M user in every account. That multiplies long-term keys, and when someone leaves, every one of those keys must be found. With federation, people sign in once, and accounts only ever see roles.

People are not the only principals. The order A P I running on our app servers also needs to call A W S: it reads product files from S three and sends order events to a queue. The wrong way is to put an access key in a configuration file on the server. The right way is a role. A role is an identity with no password and no key of its own; instead, principals that the role trusts can become it for a while. Every role has two policies, and the board shows both. On the left is the trust policy, the role's front door. It says that only the E C two service, e c two dot amazon a w s dot com, may call s t s assume role on it. On the right is the permissions policy, which says what a session of the role may do: get objects from the catalogue bucket, and send messages to the order events queue. The commands below create the role from those two files, then wrap it in an instance profile, which is how a role is attached to E C two instances. On the server, E C two assumes the role, the instance metadata service version two serves the temporary keys, and the S D K finds them without a single key in our code. The Security Token Service issues these keys, and they expire; an assume role session lasts one hour by default and at most twelve, and on an instance fresh keys arrive before the old ones expire. The misconception is that the trust policy grants access. It does not. It only says who may walk through the front door; what they can do inside is decided by the permissions policy. A role is two policies: who may become it, and what it may then do.

Now let's read a policy properly, because every permission in A W S comes down to statements like these. Each statement answers four questions. Effect: is this an allow or a deny? Action: which A P I calls, written as the service prefix, a colon, and the operation name, like s three get object. Resource: which resources, named by A R N, where a star matches any run of characters. And condition: an optional extra test on the request itself. Here is the order A P I's policy after one change. The app now lists the products in the catalogue, so it needs a second statement. Read them in turn. ReadProducts allows get object on every object whose key starts with products slash. ListProducts allows list bucket, and notice its resource: it is the bucket's own A R N, with no slash and no star, because listing is an action on the bucket, not on an object. Its condition narrows it further: the request's prefix must start with products. SendOrderEvents allows one action on one queue. That difference between the bucket and its objects is the classic mistake. Granting s three star on the bucket's A R N does not reach the objects inside it; objects have their own A R Ns, the bucket name followed by slash and the key, and an object action needs a resource that matches them. So a statement applies to a request only when the action, the resource and every condition all match, and then its effect counts.

With statements in hand, we can predict any decision. Start from the default: every request is denied unless something allows it. Then A W S gathers every policy that applies to the request. If any of them contains an explicit deny that matches, the answer is deny, full stop. If not, at least one allow must match, from an identity policy or a resource policy. And some policy types only cap the result. A permissions boundary, an organization's service control policy, or a session policy can take permissions away, but none of them can grant anything on its own. Let's test it. We add one statement to the order A P I's policy, DenyDrafts, which denies get object on anything under products slash drafts. Now read the matrix. Product one thousand and one is allowed by ReadProducts. The draft product two thousand matches ReadProducts too, but it also matches DenyDrafts, and the deny wins. Private slash costs dot c s v matches no statement at all, so it is an implicit deny. Putting an object is an implicit deny as well, because nothing allows put object. Sending an order event is allowed. These outcomes were checked by running the requests in an emulator with this exact policy. When a real request is denied, the error message names the type of policy that decided, for example an explicit deny in an identity based policy, which tells you where to look. The misconception is that a more specific allow can beat a broader deny. It cannot. Deny wins, and only then does something have to allow.

So far every policy was attached to an identity. A resource policy is attached to the resource instead: a bucket policy, a queue policy, a key policy. Because it sits on the resource, it must say who it is talking about, so it has a principal element. Our case: the audit account, seven seven seven seven, eight eight eight eight, nine nine nine nine, has an Auditor role that must read nightly reports from a bucket in production. On the left is the bucket policy in production. It names the Auditor role's A R N and allows get object on the reports. On the right is the Auditor role's own identity policy in the audit account, allowing the same read. Now the table. Within one account, an allow from either side is enough: an identity policy alone, or a resource policy alone. Across accounts, it is different. A W S evaluates the request in both accounts, and both must allow. The bucket owner must name the caller, and the caller's account must permit its principal to make the call. Remove either policy and the auditor is denied. There are exceptions even within one account: a role can only be assumed if its trust policy allows it, and a K M S key is only usable if its key policy permits it. The same idea governs services talking to services. When S three sends event notifications to an S Q S queue, the queue's resource policy must allow the S three service, and it should be scoped to our bucket with a source A R N condition, so that no one else's bucket can use that trust. The misconception is that A W S services are trusted automatically. They are not. Across accounts, and between services, both owners must agree.

Inside one account, separating development from production depends on every policy being written perfectly. Accounts give a stronger boundary. Resources, permissions and service quotas all belong to an account, so an account is the hardest wall A W S offers. A W S Organizations groups accounts together. One account, the management account, creates the organization; it should do little else. Accounts are placed in organisational units, O Us, which can be nested, and policies attach to an O U once and apply to every account below it. The whole organization pays one consolidated bill, while costs remain visible per account. Here is the shop's structure. At the root sits the management account. A Security O U holds the audit account, which will collect logs and run security tools. A Workloads O U contains two O Us, Prod and Dev, each with one account. Now read the table of what this separates. Permissions: an administrator in dev has no rights in production unless production grants them. Resources: a script that deletes every bucket it can see in dev cannot see production's buckets. Quotas: a load test in dev cannot use up production's limits. Bills: each account's cost is visible on its own. The misconception is that tags or naming conventions separate environments. Tags are labels; a policy mistake crosses them easily. Accounts are walls. So give each environment its own account, and group them with O Us.

The last layer is guardrails: limits set once, at the organization, that no account can exceed. There are two kinds. A service control policy, an S C P, limits what principals in member accounts can do. A resource control policy, an R C P, limits what anyone can do to resources in member accounts, whoever the caller is. Neither of them ever grants a permission, and neither affects the management account, which is one more reason to keep that account almost empty. On the left is an S C P attached to the Workloads O U. It denies every action outside E U west two, except the listed global services such as I A M, Route fifty three and CloudFront, which are not tied to our Region. On the right is an R C P. It denies any S three access by principals outside our organization, unless an A W S service is acting for us. Even if someone later writes a bucket policy that opens a bucket to the world, this guardrail still blocks outsiders. R C Ps launched for S three, S T S, K M S, S Q S and Secrets Manager, and have since added services, so check the current list. The table puts every policy type in one place: only identity and resource policies grant; boundaries, S C Ps and R C Ps only limit. Finally, ownership of the audit trail. Rather than run security tools from the management account, a member account, our audit account, is made the delegated administrator for services such as GuardDuty and Security Hub, and it collects the organization's logs. The misconception is that an S C P gives production its permissions. It does not; roles still need an allow. Guardrails cap, and only identity and resource policies grant. Authorisation still says nothing about whether a request can reach its target, so next we trace the network paths requests must travel.

Before we can trace a request through a network, we need its addresses. An I P version four address is thirty two bits, written as four numbers, like ten dot twenty dot eleven dot thirty seven. A range of addresses is written in C I D R notation: an address, a slash, and a number saying how many leading bits are fixed. A slash sixteen fixes sixteen bits and leaves sixteen free, which is sixty five thousand five hundred and thirty six addresses. A slash twenty four leaves eight bits free, which is two hundred and fifty six. Addresses find a machine; ports find a program on it. H T T P S listens on four four three. Our app servers listen on eight zero eight zero, PostgreSQL on five four three two, and D N S on fifty three. T C P gives an ordered, acknowledged stream; U D P sends single packets, which is why D N S often uses it. Now the shop's plan, computed rather than asserted. The production V P C is ten dot twenty dot zero dot zero slash sixteen. The code cuts it into nine slash twenty four subnets: public, app and data tiers, one of each per Availability Zone. A W S reserves five addresses in every subnet, the first four and the last, so each slash twenty four has two hundred and fifty one usable addresses. The code also finds which subnet holds ten dot twenty dot eleven dot thirty seven, app b, and confirms that no two ranges overlap. The misconception is that a bigger range is always safer. The real risk is overlap: two networks using the same addresses can never be joined later. So plan ranges once, check them with code, and never let them overlap.

A V P C, a virtual private cloud, is your own private network inside one Region. It owns an address range, and every network resource you create lives inside it. A V P C spans all the Availability Zones of its Region, but a subnet does not. A subnet is a slice of the V P C's range placed in exactly one zone. And the thing that actually connects a server to a subnet is its elastic network interface, an E N I, which sits in one subnet and takes its private address from that subnet's range. Look at the layout for shop prod. The V P C is ten dot twenty dot zero dot zero slash sixteen, in E U west two. Each of the three zones gets three subnets, one per tier: a public subnet for the load balancer and N A T gateways, an app subnet for the order A P I servers, and a data subnet for the database. So the app server in zone b has an E N I in app b, with the address ten dot twenty dot eleven dot thirty seven from our calculation. Why tiers? Because each tier will get different routes and different filters, and those attach to subnets and interfaces. And why repeat them in every zone? Because, as we saw in chapter one, surviving the loss of a zone means having capacity in the others. The misconception is that one subnet can span the Region. It cannot; if you want a tier in three zones, you create three subnets. So: one V P C per environment, and one subnet per tier per zone.

Addresses say where a packet is going; route tables say which way to send it. Every subnet is associated with one route table, a list of destination ranges and targets. Every table contains a local route for the V P C's own range, so instances in the same V P C can always reach each other's addresses. An internet gateway, attached to the V P C, is its door to the internet, and a default route, zero dot zero dot zero dot zero slash zero, pointing at it is what makes a subnet public. Look at the two tables. The public subnets send everything outside the V P C to the internet gateway. The app subnets have three routes: local, a route to the development V P C through a peering connection, which we meet in section nine, and a default route to a N A T gateway, which is the next section. When a destination matches more than one route, the most specific one wins, the one with the longest prefix. The code applies that rule. Ten dot twenty dot twenty dot fifteen, a database address, matches local. Ten dot thirty dot four dot nine matches both the slash sixteen to dev and the default route, and the slash sixteen is more specific, so it goes over the peering. The payment provider's address matches only the default, so it goes to the N A T gateway. The misconception is that the order of rows in the table decides. It does not; the prefix length decides. So to predict a packet's next hop, find the subnet's route table and pick the longest matching prefix.

Now an incident, the one the plan asks us to diagnose. The order A P I runs in the private app subnets, and it must call a payment provider at api dot payments dot example dot com. The call times out after five seconds. Read the route table, as the comment does: rt app a contains only the local route. There is no path out of the V P C at all, so the packets have nowhere to go, and a timeout, rather than a refusal, is the typical symptom. We do not want the app servers to be reachable from the internet, so we will not give them public addresses or a route to the internet gateway. Instead we add a N A T gateway. It sits in a public subnet, it has an Elastic I P, and it translates the private servers' outgoing connections so they appear to come from that one public address. The commands allocate the address, create the N A T gateway in public a, and add a default route from the app subnet's table to it. Replies to connections the servers started come back through the N A T; connections started from the internet cannot come in. N A T gateways are zonal by default, so one per zone keeps each zone's outbound traffic independent of the others. Now the table. A server in a public subnet with a public address can call out and be called. In a public subnet without a public address, it can do neither. Private with no N A T route, neither. Private with a N A T route, outbound only. The misconception is that putting something in a public subnet makes it reachable. It also needs a public address, and the filters in the next section must allow the traffic. Routes and addresses decide direction, and N A T only works one way.

Routes decide where a packet can go. Filters decide whether it is allowed. A W S gives us two. A security group is attached to a network interface. It contains only allow rules, all of them considered together, and it is stateful: if a request is allowed in, its reply is allowed out automatically. A network A C L is attached to a subnet. It has both allow and deny rules, evaluated in order from the lowest rule number, first match wins, and it is stateless, so the reply needs its own rule, usually on the client's ephemeral ports. Most designs do their real filtering with security groups, and here is the shop's chain. The load balancer's group, s g a l b, allows port four four three from anywhere, because shoppers are anywhere. The app servers' group allows port eight zero eight zero, but only from s g a l b. Notice the source is not an address range; it is another security group, meaning any interface carrying that group. When the load balancer adds nodes, the rule still fits. The database group allows five four three two only from the app group. The request in the middle is exactly that app rule, validated against the E C two A P I. So the database cannot be reached even by something else inside the V P C that is not an app server. The misconception is that a route means traffic flows. A route is necessary, but every filter on the way, security groups and network A C Ls, in both directions where they are stateless, must also allow it. Routes say where; filters say whether.

Shoppers do not type addresses; they type shop dot example dot com. D N S turns that name into an address. The browser asks a recursive resolver, usually run by the shopper's network. If the resolver has no cached answer, it asks the root servers, then the dot com servers, and finally the authoritative servers for example dot com. Ours is a Route fifty three public hosted zone, the container for the domain's records. The answer comes back with a time to live, a T T L, and the resolver caches it for that long. The record on the right is how we publish the shop. It is an upsert, create or replace, of an A record for shop dot example dot com. But instead of a fixed address, it is an alias: it points at the load balancer's D N S name, and Route fifty three answers with the load balancer's current addresses, which can change. Evaluate target health means Route fifty three will consider whether the target is healthy. This request was validated against the Route fifty three A P I; the zone identifiers are placeholders. Below it are the routing policies, which decide which answer to give when there is more than one: simple, weighted, for sending ten percent of users to a new version, latency, failover to a secondary, and geolocation. The misconception is that a D N S change takes effect at once. Resolvers all over the world keep the old answer until its T T L expires. So treat names as cached pointers, and plan changes around their T T Ls.

So far we have made the request reachable. That says nothing about whether anyone on the path can read it. T L S does two jobs on a single hop: it encrypts the traffic, and, with a certificate, it proves that the server really is shop dot example dot com. A W S Certificate Manager, A C M, issues certificates for A W S endpoints and renews them automatically once the domain is validated, here through D N S. Look at the path. The browser's connection uses T L S one point three and ends at the load balancer. That is the termination point. The commands request the certificate and attach it to an H T T P S listener on port four four three with a T L S one point three security policy. The certificate must live in the load balancer's own Region, E U west two; CloudFront, by contrast, only uses certificates from U S east one. After the load balancer, the request travels to the app server on port eight zero eight zero, and unless the target group is set to H T T P S, that hop is plain H T T P inside the V P C. The database hop is encrypted only if the application's database client requires T L S. The table makes each hop a separate decision. The misconception is that traffic inside a V P C is encrypted anyway. Being able to reach something tells you nothing about encryption. So decide each hop explicitly, and write down where T L S terminates.

The load balancer is where many app servers become one service. An application load balancer understands H T T P, so it can route by path or host; a network load balancer forwards T C P and U D P with very low overhead. Behind a listener sits a target group, the set of servers that should receive traffic. Health checks decide which members actually get it. The command creates the shop's target group and sets every health check value explicitly rather than relying on defaults: check the slash health path every ten seconds, mark a target unhealthy after two failures in a row, and healthy again after three successes. Now the timeline, computed by the code with exactly those numbers. App three breaks at time zero. The checks at five and fifteen seconds fail, so at fifteen seconds it is marked unhealthy and traffic stops. Until then, roughly fifteen seconds of requests went to a broken server. It is fixed at sixty seconds, and three passing checks bring it back at eighty five seconds. Meanwhile the evening's five hundred and sixty requests a second are spread across fewer targets: about ninety three each across six, about one hundred and twelve each across five. Our servers handle one hundred and fifty, so the others absorb it. The misconception is that a failing target disappears instantly. The interval times the threshold sets the delay in both directions. So set those thresholds on purpose, and keep spare capacity for the moments a target is out.

The last piece of the network is private paths. Today, when the app servers read product files from S three, the traffic leaves through the N A T gateway, as if S three were any other internet service. A V P C endpoint gives it a private path instead. A gateway endpoint for S three adds a route to the subnet's table pointing at S three's address list, and it has no endpoint charge. Its endpoint policy, on the board, limits it to the shop's buckets, so the endpoint cannot be used to copy data somewhere else. It was checked against the I A M action and resource reference. Interface endpoints do the same for many other services, by placing a network interface in your subnet, with an hourly charge. Connecting networks to each other is next in the table. V P C peering joins exactly two V P Cs, like our route to the development V P C, and it is not transitive: if A peers with B and B with C, A still cannot reach C through B. A transit gateway is a hub for many V P Cs. To reach the shop's office network, a Site-to-Site V P N runs I P sec over the internet, with two tunnels per connection, and Direct Connect provides a private, dedicated link. The misconception is that Direct Connect is encrypted. It is private, but it is not encrypted by default; you add MACsec on supported links, or run a V P N over it. Every path has a boundary, whether transitivity, cost or encryption. With request paths established, next we choose where application processing runs and how capacity changes.
